title: The Lord is my shepherd (Psalm 23)
hook: sung at the third Shabbat meal and read at funerals

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm eight under the stars. Your line was a little lower than angels. Did you feel small, and crowned? Today, a psalm sung at a table and read at a grave. Day three hundred seventeen.

It's late on a Saturday afternoon. The light is going gold. Shabbat is almost over, and around a table, people eat a last small meal, and someone starts to sing, slowly: Mizmor le-David. A psalm of David. The Lord is my shepherd. Change the scene: a cemetery, a family at a graveside, and someone reading the same words. The same psalm at the gentlest hour of the week, and at the hardest hour of a life. Today: Psalm twenty-three.
screen: `SHABBAT'S LAST GOLDEN HOUR.` → `A GRAVESIDE.` → `THE SAME PSALM AT BOTH.`

segments.voice: It starts: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." In Hebrew, lo echsar: I will not lack. Not I'll have everything. I won't be missing what I need. The psalm is headed for David, who, in the Book of Samuel, was a shepherd before he was a king. A shepherd in dry hill country has to find grass and water. So: green pastures, and still waters, in Hebrew mei menuchot, waters of rest. He restores my soul. He leads me on straight paths. Then comes the valley. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, "I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me." Listen to what just happened. Up to now, the psalm has been talking about God: He leads me, He restores me. In the dark valley, it switches. Now it talks to God: You are with me. Before the valley, God is described. From the valley on, God is addressed: Thou art with me, Thou preparest a table. Some readers hear in that turn why this psalm belongs at gravesides. And it is sung as Shabbat fades, just before a new week begins. Then the scene changes again: a table set in front of me, a cup that overflows, and a home in the house of the Lord for long days. The psalm doesn't pretend there is no valley. It walks straight through it, with company.
screen: `LO ECHSAR: I WILL NOT LACK.` · `GREEN PASTURES, STILL WATERS.` · `IN THE VALLEY: FROM HE TO YOU.` · `A TABLE, AN OVERFLOWING CUP.` · then, large: `I SHALL NOT WANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read it slowly once. If you can, find Psalm twenty-three. It's only six verses. Read it aloud, slowly, pausing after each line. If you can't, hear the first line again and let it sit: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. Settle, and breathe. Notice where your own life is right now: the pasture, the still water, or the valley. Wherever you are, stay with the line that fits. If you pray, you can say it as your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Lord is my shepherd. Psalm twenty-three: green pastures, still waters, and the dark valley where the psalm turns and speaks to God directly.
screen: `THE LORD IS MY SHEPHERD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I shall not want. Today, when you feel something missing, pause and name one thing you're not lacking. Day three hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Psalm 23 is sung at the third Shabbat meal, and in some communities on Friday night too; it is also read at funerals, at the unveiling of a gravestone and when visiting the sick.

trapdoor: what you thought: a funeral psalm.
what it means: a shepherd's song of trust that walks straight through the dark, with company.
what a scholar hears: tzalmavet is traditionally read as tzel mavet, shadow of death, and by some scholars as deep darkness, and the shift from third to second person comes exactly at that verse.
